rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause can explain the preceding wording because it implies speech without an explicit saying verb.
rows.anchor: ما يتضمن معنى القول دون حروفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parse makes it a genitive substitute for the pronoun in ‘what He enjoined’; the relative clause retains a referent because the replaced element is conceptually omitted.
rows.anchor: على أنه بدل من ضمير ( به ) ولا يلزمه بقاء الموصول بلا عائد

rows.speaker: شيخ الإسلام
rows.claim: Sheikh al-Islam objects that this parsing removes the command from revelation to Muhammad and implies the prohibition addresses earlier prophets, though it is intended for Muhammad’s community.
rows.anchor: مع إفاضته إلى خروجه عن حيز الأيحاء إلى النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause may instead be a substitute for the word ‘religion.’
rows.anchor: وجوز كونه بدلا من ( الدين ) ويجوز كون ( أن ) مفسره

rows.speaker: غير واحد من الأجلة
rows.claim: Several eminent scholars take the command and prohibition to address Muhammad and his followers as well as earlier prophets and their communities.
rows.anchor: على ما اختاره غير واحد من الأجلة شامل للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأتباعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi finds the prohibition most plausibly addressed to Muhammad’s community, the people who became divided; addressing earlier prophets’ communities would be strained.
rows.anchor: وأنهم المتفرقون ثم بين ما استظهره وسنشير إليه إن شاء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Religion here means the shared fundamentals; the prohibition is against accepting some and rejecting others, not differing over subsidiary laws that varied between communities.
rows.anchor: الذي هو عبارة عما تقدم من الأصول بأن يأتي به بعض ولا يأتي بعض

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some include certain subsidiary matters among the fundamentals intended by ‘religion’ here.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم أدخل بعض الفروع في أصول الدين المرادة هنا من الدين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says every prophet was commanded to establish prayer, give alms, affirm God, and obey Him; these make up establishing religion.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد : لم يبعث نبي إلا أمر بأقامة الصلاة وأيتاء الزكاة والإقرار بالله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi describes religious prescriptions developing from Adam’s basic guidance, through Noah’s prohibitions and duties, then being reinforced by successive prophets until the final law.
rows.anchor: وقال الحافظ أبو بكر بن العربي : لم يكن مع آدم عليه السلام إلا بنوه

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says the prophets shared one religion in fundamentals, including worship, moral virtues, trustworthiness, kinship, and avoiding arrogance, adultery, cruelty, and disgraceful conduct.
rows.anchor: فمعنى الآية شرعنا لكم ماشرعنا للأنبياء دينا واحدا في الأصول وهي التوحيد والصلاة

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi glosses establishing religion as making it endure continuously, without disagreement or instability.
rows.anchor: اجعلوه قائما أي دائما مستمرا من غير خلاف فيه ولا اضطراب انتهى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi qualifies Ibn al-Arabi’s list: prayer, alms, fasting, and pilgrimage must mean these rites generically, since their specific forms belong to Muhammad’s community and the sura is Meccan.
rows.anchor: ولعله أراد بالصلاة والزكاة والصيام والحج مطلقا لا ما نعرفه منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Religions certainly differed in subsidiary laws; specific alms and Ramadan fasting were instituted in Medina, and pilgrimage apparently was not prescribed for Moses’ and Jesus’ communities or most earlier peoples.
rows.anchor: وبالجملة لا شك في اختلاف الأديان في الفروع نعم لا يبعد اتفاقها فيما هو من مكارم الأخلاق

words: كَبُرَ عَلَى ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ مَا تَدْعُوهُمْ إِلَيْهِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What grievously burdens the polytheists is the Prophet’s continuing call to monotheism and rejection of idols, the foremost principle and their greatest difficulty.
rows.anchor: على سبيل الأستمرار التجددي من التوحيد ورفض عبادة الأصنام ويشعر بإرادته التعبير

words: كَبُرَ عَلَى ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ مَا تَدْعُوهُمْ إِلَيْهِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible referent is the call to establish religion and avoid division.
rows.anchor: أو ما تدعوهم إليه من إقامة الدين وعدم التفرق فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s choosing and guiding those who turn to Him consoles the Prophet: some among those called will respond.
rows.anchor: تسلية له صلى الله عليه وسلم بأن منهم من تجنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi prefers both pronouns ‘to Him’ to refer to God: He selects through divine grace and guides through direction and enabling those who turn to Him; the chosen and guided are distinct groups within the people of religion.
rows.anchor: قال في الكشف أظهر وأملأ بالفائدة أما الثاني فللدلالة على أن أهل الاجتباء غير أهل الاهتداء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some refer both pronouns to religion, understanding ‘choose’ as gathering people to faith, which suits the preceding mention of division.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من اختار جعله للدين لمناسبة معنوية هي اتحاد المتفرق فيه والمجتمع عليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari derives ‘choose’ from gathering and refers the pronoun to religion; Alusi calls this a surface-level reading based on the preceding theme of unity.
rows.anchor: والزمخشري اختار كونه من الجباية بمعنى الجمع وعود الضمير على الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ‘choose’ is more commonly used for selection, making the people of religion God’s elect, chosen for Himself.
rows.anchor: فلأن الاجتباء بمعنى الاصطفاء أكثر استعمالا ولأنه يدل أن أهل الدين هم صفوة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reading takes the call as belief in the prophetic message: the polytheists resent the Prophet’s selection for revelation, and God’s choice answers them as in ‘God knows best where to place His message.’
rows.anchor: على معنى ما تدعوهم إلى الإيمان به والمراد به الرسالة أي ثقلت عليهم رسالتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi prefers the earlier explanation of the call as monotheism and establishing religion over the alternative focused on the Prophet’s appointment.
rows.anchor: وما قدمنا أظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one parse, ‘whatever you were given’ is a relative clause with an omitted object pronoun, and its result clause takes fa because the relative has conditional force.
rows.anchor: ودخلت الفاء لتضمنها معنى الشرط وقال أبو حيان

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan instead parses ‘whatever’ as a conditional, the second object of ‘were given,’ with ‘of anything’ explaining it.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان : هي شرطية مفعول ثان لأوتيتم و ( من شيء ) بيان لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every worldly provision is only enjoyment during earthly life; God’s reward is better in pure benefit and more enduring because it does not vanish.
rows.anchor: أي فهو متاعها تتمتعون به مدة حياتكم فيها جواب الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘What is with God’ is relative, but its predicate lacks fa: being better is already understood from being with God, unlike what others possess.
rows.anchor: لأن الظاهر أن ( ما ) فيه موصولة وإنما لم يؤت بالفاء في خبرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘For those who believe’ may modify ‘more enduring,’ or its lām may explain who owns the blessing, with an omitted predicate.
rows.anchor: إما متعلق بأبقى أو اللام لبيان من له هذه النعمة فهو خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers rely on their Lord alone, not on anyone else.
rows.anchor: لا على غيره تعالى أصلا

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Alusi reports from Ali that Abu Bakr gave all his wealth in God’s cause, drawing criticism from Muslims and disbelievers; this verse was then revealed. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وعن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه اجتمع لأبي بكر رضي الله تعالى عنه مال

words: وَلَئِن سَأَلْتَهُم مَّنْ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question is coordinated with the preceding address; the verses beginning ‘How many messengers We sent’ interrupt to affirm the point and console the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والآيتان أعني قوله تعالى : وكم أرسلنا اعتراض لأفادة التقرير والتسلية كما سمعت

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says disbelievers attribute creation to God, who in reality has these attributes, without necessarily uttering the titles or consciously describing Him by them; Alusi accepts this as sufficient.
rows.anchor: ذكره الزمخشري فيما نسب إليه وهذا حسب وله نظير عرفا

rows.speaker: ابن المنير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Munir parses ‘the Mighty, the Knowing’ as the answerers’ words and the following material as God’s continuation; al-Kashf says this yields the same result as the alternative analysis.
rows.anchor: والأظهر من حيث اللفظ ما ذكره ابن المنير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi finds Ibn al-Munir’s division more apparent from the wording, though either account yields quoted speech supplemented by God.
rows.anchor: والأظهر من حيث اللفظ ما ذكره ابن المنير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Ibn al-Munir’s reading, the shift to ‘We brought forth’ in verse 11 falls naturally after a change of speaker; Moses’ speech followed by ‘We brought forth’ is a parallel.
rows.anchor: ونظير ذلك قوله تعالى حكاية عن موسى عليه السلام : ( لا يضل ربي ولا ينسى )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the verb emphasizes creation and matches the question in meaning, as Abu Hayyan argues, though not in grammatical form.
rows.anchor: وفي إعادة الفعل في الجوانب اعتناء بشأنه ومطابقته للسؤال من حيث المعنى

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan notes that verbal form would not match the question grammatically: ‘who’ is the subject, so a matching answer would make ‘the Mighty, the Knowing’ the nominal subject.
rows.anchor: لأن من مبتدأ فلو طابق في اللفظ لكان بالاسم مبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth is made a leveled, prepared place for people to settle; its spherical shape does not conflict with this because of its immense size.
rows.anchor: مكانا ممهدا أي موطأ ومآله بسطها لكم تستقرون فيها ولا ينافي ذلك كرتها

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: Asim reads the word without an alif.
rows.anchor: وعن عاصم أنه قرأ ( مهدا ) بدون ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paths are routes to destinations and can also lead by reflection to monotheism, the primary goal.
rows.anchor: أي لكي تهتدوا بسلوكها إلى مقاصدكم أو بالتفكر فيها إلى التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain falls in a measure set by divine will, wisdom, and interests; only God knows precisely how much falls each year.
rows.anchor: أي بمقدار تقتضيه المشيئة المبنية على الحكم والمصالح ولا يعلم مقدار ما ينزل

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Bahr glosses the measure as a decree fixed in pre-eternity; Alusi prefers the measure determined by divine wisdom.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر بقدر أي بقضاء وحتم في الأزل والأول أولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi doubts claims that the contemporary ‘audometer’ precisely measures annual rainfall even in one small locality, much less everywhere.
rows.anchor: المسماة بالاود وميتر يزعمون أنه يعرف بها مقدار المطر النازل في كل بلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God revived the barren town by the rain; it had no growth or plants at all.
rows.anchor: خالية عن النماء والنبات بالكلية

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وعيسى
rows.claim: Abu Jaafar and Isa read ‘mayyitan’ with doubled yāʾ; the masculine form treats ‘town’ as land or place.
rows.anchor: بالتشديد وتذكيره لأن البلدة في معنى البلد والمكان

rows.speaker: الجلبي
rows.claim: Al-Jalabi suggests that the feminine ‘town’ with masculine ‘dead’ may signal the extreme limit of its lifelessness; Alusi says this is possible.
rows.anchor: قال الجلبي : لا يبعد والله تعالى أعلم أن يكون تأنيث البلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of the town as dead uses either an implicit or explicit metaphor.
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام استعارة مكنية أو تصريحية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift to first-person plural highlights divine care for reviving the earth and signals the act’s importance.
rows.anchor: إلى نون العظمة لإظهار كمال العناية بأمر الأحياء والأشعار بعظم خطره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As vegetation emerges from the earth, people will be raised alive from their graves; ‘likewise’ modifies an omitted verbal noun meaning resurrection like this.
rows.anchor: أيتبعثون من قبوركم أحياء وفي التعبير عن إخراج النبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling plant growth ‘revival’ and resurrection ‘being brought forth’ magnifies vegetation and makes resurrection seem less difficult, rebutting deniers.
rows.anchor: تفخيم لشأن الأنبات وتهوين لأمرالبعث وفي ذلك من الرد على منكر ما فيه

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب وعبد الله بن جبير وعيسى وابن عامر والأخوان
rows.claim: These readers pronounce ‘tukhrajūn’ in the active voice.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن وثاب وعبد الله بن جبير وعيسى وابن عامر والأخوان ( تخرجون ) مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Pairs’ means all classes of created things, rather than pairs in the narrower familiar sense.
rows.anchor: أي أصناف المخلوقات فالزوج هنا بمعنى الصنف لا بمعناه المشهور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the pairs as kinds and varieties, such as sweet and sour, white and black, and male and female.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس الأزواج الضروب والأنواع كالحلو والحامض والأبيض والأسود

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say everything besides God is paired because it has an opposite, while God alone is free of counterparts; Alusi questions whether this applies universally.
rows.anchor: وقيل : كل ما سوى الله سبحانه زوج لأنه لا يخلو من المقابل كفوق وتحت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A possible basis for that view is that God is one in every respect and uncomposed, unlike contingent beings, whether material or immaterial.
rows.anchor: بناه على أن الواجب جل شأنه واحد من جميع الجهات لا تركيب فيه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘What you ride’ is a relative clause with omitted referent; ships take a preposition with ‘ride’ while mounts take a direct object, so the direct construction dominates by strength, or animals are preferred over ships.
rows.anchor: فما موصولة والعائد محذوف والركوب بالنظر إلى الفلكي تعدى بواسطة الحرف وهو في

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording uses ‘settle’ for all conveyances though it particularly suits mounts; the singular pronoun follows ‘what you ride’ grammatically, while plural ‘backs’ follows its meaning.
rows.anchor: حيث عبر عن القرار على الجميع بالاستواء المخصوص بالدواب والضمير لما تركبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi takes the lām as purposive; al-Hawfi allows a consequential lām.
rows.anchor: أن لام ( لتستووا ) لام كي وقال الحوفي : من أثبت لام للصيرورة جاز له أن يقول به هنا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya calls it an imperative lām, which Alusi regards as unlikely because the second-person tāʾ form is rare.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية : هي لام الأمر وفيه بعد من حيث استعماله أمر المخاطب بتاء الخطاب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj considers the second-person imperative a good usage; Abu Hayyan prefers the purposive lām and reports it as the majority grammarians’ view.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج : إنها لغة جيدة وأبو حيان على الأول وحكاه عن جمهور النحويين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Examples cited for the rare imperative include an irregular reading, poetry, and a Prophetic phrase that hadith scholars may have transmitted by meaning.
rows.anchor: لا تكاد تحتفظ إلا في قراءة شاذة نحو ( فبذلك فلتفرحوا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remember the blessing inwardly, acknowledging and esteeming it, then praise God aloud; this is gratitude, with inward acknowledgment part of proper remembrance.
rows.anchor: أي تذكروها بقلوبكم معترفين بها مستعظمين لها ثم تحمدوا عليها بألسنتكم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says remembrance entails heart awareness while the intended act is verbal praise, with both together its fullest form; Alusi calls this sound too.
rows.anchor: الزمخشري أن الذكر يتضمن شعور القلب والمراد على اللسان فنزل على أكمل أحواله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Those who allow a shared word to bear both meanings understand remembrance as inward and verbal.
rows.anchor: ومن جوز استعمال المشترك في معنييه جوز هنا أن يراد بالذكر الذكر القلبي والذكر اللساني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The utterance declares God exalted for making the conveyance tame; ‘this’ depicts the situation to heighten wonder, not belittle it, and its declarative wording implies a request to say it.
rows.anchor: أي وتقولواسبحان الذي ذلله وجعله منقادا لنا متعجبين من ذلك وليس الإشارة للتحقير

rows.speaker: أبو مجلز
rows.claim: Abu Majliz reports that Husayn ibn Ali corrected a rider by first praising God for Islam, Muhammad, and belonging to the best community, then reciting the travel formula; this points to Islam as the blessing. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: أخرج عبد بن حميد وابن جرير وابن المنذر عن أبي مجلز قال : رأى الحسين بن علي

rows.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir reports that Shahr ibn Hawshab interpreted the blessing as Islam.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر عن شهر بن حوشب أنه فسرها بنعمة الإسلام

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report from Ali, graded authentic by al-Tirmidhi, gives the mounting supplication: say ‘in God’s name’ at the stirrup, praise and magnify God three times, recite the verses, then seek forgiveness; Ali says the Prophet did likewise and describes God’s delight at the plea.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أحمد وأبو داود والترمذي وصححه والنسائي وجماعة عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report in Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Dawud, and al-Darimi says the Prophet praised, glorified, and magnified God three times when mounting his camel to travel, then recited these verses. No grading is stated here.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أخرجه مسلم والترمذي وأبو داود والدارمي عن ابن عمر أن رسول الله

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report transmitted by Ahmad and others says every camel has a devil on its hump, so riders should invoke God’s name when mounting.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أخرجه أحمد وغيره عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : ما من بعير إلا في ذروته شيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remembrance and formula apply to ships as well as animals; some say ‘In God’s name is its course and anchorage’ when embarking and pray for a blessed landing when disembarking.
rows.anchor: وظاهر النظم الجليل أن تذكر النعمة والقول المذكور لا يخصان ركوب الأنعام بل يعم إنها والفلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We could not master it’ means we lacked strength to control the mount or ship; God alone subdued and controlled it.
rows.anchor: ما يضبط به الدابة والفلك وإنما الله تعالى هو الذيسخر ذلك وضبطه لنا

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub cites Amr ibn Maʿdikarib’s line as evidence that the root can mean being able or matched in strength.
rows.anchor: وأنشد قطرب لعمرو ابن معدي كرب : لقد علم القبائل ما عقيل لنا في نائبات بمقرنينا

rows.speaker: ابن هرمة
rows.claim: Ibn Harma’s verse is cited as evidence for being capable of what one is made to bear.
rows.anchor: قال ابن هرمة : وأقرنت ما حملتني ولقلما يطلق احتمال الصدياد عد والهجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The underlying image is finding something as one’s peer: a difficult mount cannot be a weak person’s equal, and ‘qarn’ can mean the binding rope.
rows.anchor: وحقيقة أقرنه وجده قرينته وما يقرن به لأن الصعب لا يكون قرينة للضعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A line about a young camel restrained by a rope shows it cannot withstand the charge of powerful mature camels, illustrating the root’s binding sense.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر : وابن اللبون إذا ما لز في قرن لم يستطع صولة البزل القناعيس

rows.speaker: سليمان بن يسار
rows.claim: Ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir report that a traveler boasted he could master his powerful camel after reciting the verse; it bucked him down and broke his neck. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: أخرج عبد بن حميد وابن المنذر عن سليمان بن يسار أن قوما كانوا في سفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading doubles the rāʾ, with either fatḥa or kasra; both forms mean the same as the undoubled reading.
rows.anchor: وقريء ( مقرنين ) بتشديد الراء مع فتحها وكسرها وهما بمعنى المخفف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We will return’ means returning to God; a rider should make travel a reminder of the greater return, order conduct by that awareness, and ride only for a lawful purpose because riding is perilous.
rows.anchor: وفيه إيذان بأن حق الراكب أن يتأمل فيما يلابسه من السير ويتذكر منه المسافرة العظمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Likewise’ continues the preceding point about disbelievers’ inability to argue and their retreat to imitation; inherited blind following is an old error.
rows.anchor: أي والأمر كما ذكر من عجزهم عن الحجة مطلقا وتشبثهم بذيل التقليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse resumes to explain that earlier generations also had no considered proof from their own predecessors.
rows.anchor: استئناف مبين لذلك دال على أن التقليد فيما بينهم ضلال قديم لأسلافهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The affluent are singled out because luxury and love of idleness diverted them from examining inherited beliefs.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص المترفين بتلك المقالة للإيذان بأن التنعم وحب البطالة صرفهم عن النظر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd identify the Prophet’s people as Quraysh; the Quran is a great honor for them. Alusi prefers this interpretation.
rows.anchor: هم قريش على ما روي عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة والسدي وابن زيد

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ali and Ibn Abbas says the Prophet sought support among Meccan tribes and promised victory; asked who would rule after him, he withheld an answer until this verse, then named Quraysh, who accepted only after the Ansar did. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن عدي وابن مردويه عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما قالا

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
rows.claim: A report from Adi ibn Hatim says God knew the Prophet’s love for his people and gave them glad tidings through this verse, making Quraysh renowned; it also praises Quraysh and mentions the truthful one and martyr among them. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: قال ألا إن الله تعالى علم ما في قلبي من حبي لقومي فبشرني فيهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view takes ‘your people’ as all Arabs because the Quran came in their language, with honor concentrated increasingly among closer groups, especially Quraysh and Banu Hashim.
rows.anchor: وقيل هم العرب مطلقا لما أن القرآن نزل بلغتهم ثم يختص بذلك الشرف الأخص فالأخص

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatadah is also reported to identify the Prophet’s people as his followers from the Muslim community.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة هم مناتبعه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم من أمته

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the people are the Muslim community, making the Quran a reminder for the Prophet and his nation; Alusi favors Quraysh.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : هم الأمة والمعنى وإنه لتذكرة وموعظة لك ولأمتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the primary reading, people will be asked on Judgment Day about the Quran and whether they fulfilled its rights.
rows.anchor: يوم القيامة عنه وعن قيامكم بحقوقه

rows.speaker: الحسن والكلبي والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, and al-Zajjaj instead say people will be asked to thank God for the honor bestowed on them.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن والكلبي والزجاج : تسئلون عن شكر ما جعله الله تعالى لكم من الشرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse indicates that people naturally desire good praise and lasting renown: God presents this honor as a favor, and noble remembrance stands in for continued life.
rows.anchor: قيل إن هذه الآية تدل على أن الإنسان يرغب في الثناء الحسن والذكر الجميل

rows.speaker: ابن دريد
rows.claim: Ibn Duraid’s verse says a person lives on as a story after death and urges the listener to leave a good account.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن دريد : وإنما المرء حديث بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A following poetic saying calls the world’s finest beauty the good report that remains after a person is gone.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر إنما الدنيا محاسنها طيب ما يبقى من الخبر

rows.speaker: هلاكو
rows.claim: In an anecdote, Hulagu asks who is king; courtiers praise his conquests, but he points to the Prophet, dead for over six centuries yet named by callers to prayer five times daily, as enduring renown.
rows.anchor: ويحكى أن الطاغية هلاكو سأل أصحابه من الملك فقالوا : له أنت الذي دوخت البلاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their punishment is never eased; the root of ‘futūr’ indicates weakening in any form, as when a fever subsides briefly.
rows.anchor: والمادة بأي صيغة كانت تدل على الضعف مطلقا

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Abdullah reads ‘fīhā,’ referring to Hell rather than the punishment.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله فيها أي في جهنم

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines ‘iblās’ as grief from severe distress and says Iblis’s name derives from it, according to one account.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب : الإبلاس الحزن المعترض من شدة البأس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is also explained as silence and loss of argument: a despairing person often falls quiet and forgets what to say.
rows.anchor: ولما كان المبلس كثيرا ما يلزم السكوت وينسى ما يعنيه قيل

rows.speaker: بعض الآثار
rows.claim: An unspecified report says hunger is imposed on the people of Hell until it equals their other torment, so they call Malik. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الآثار يلقى على أهل النار الجوع حتى يعدل ما هم فيه من العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They ask Malik to request that his Lord kill them and grant relief; saying ‘your Lord’ is an appeal for help, not rejection.
rows.anchor: أي ليمتنا من قضى عليه إذا أماته ومرادهم سل ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their call can coexist with despair as they fall silent at times and cry out at others during prolonged punishment; one objection is that alternating states do not suit the continuous clause ‘they are despairing.’
rows.anchor: لأنه صراخ وتمني للموت من فرط الشدة وأما على التفسير الثاني

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another reply says the coordinating wāw does not require sequence, so calling need not follow despair; Alusi notes the circumstantial clause remains tied to their abiding state.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن نادوا معطوف بالواو وهي لا تقتضي ترتيبا ولا يخفى أن تلك الجملة حالية

rows.speaker: علي وابن مسعود وابن وثاب والأعمش
rows.claim: Ali, Ibn Masud, Ibn Waththab, and al-Aʿmash read ‘yā Māl,’ using the language that anticipates the omitted ending.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه وابن مسعود وابن وثاب والأعمش يا مال بالترخيم على لغة من ينتظر

rows.speaker: أبو السوار
rows.claim: Abu al-Sawwar reads the shortened name according to the language that does not anticipate the omitted ending.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو السوار يا مال بالترخيم أيضا لكن على لغة من لم ينتظر

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni says truncation signals collapsed strength and humbled souls, rather than deliberate stylistic flourish.
rows.anchor: وللترخيم في هذاالموضع سر وذلك أنهم لعظم ما همفيه ضعفت قواهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas objects that the people of Hell would be too occupied for the unusual shortened form; the reply is that helplessness and constriction force the truncation.
rows.anchor: ما أشغل أهل النار على الترخيم مشيرا بذلك إلى إنكارها فإن ما للتعجيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poetic shortened vocative is explained by inability and lack of room to finish the word, not intentional verbal artistry.
rows.anchor: والحق يا مال غير ما تصف بل للعجز وضيق المجال عن الإتمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Malik says they remain forever with no escape through death or otherwise; this deepens despair, and their hopelessness does not prevent the answer from tormenting them.
rows.anchor: مقيمون في العذاب أبدا لا خلاص لكم منه بموت ولا غيره وهذا تقنيط ونكاية لهم

rows.speaker: بعض الأجلة
rows.claim: Some hear mockery in ‘remaining,’ since the word can suggest a stay that ends and involves waiting; the delayed answer may heighten it.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعض الأجلة أن فيه استهزاء لأنه أقام المكث مقام الخلود والمكث يشعر بالانقطاع
